input: In this passage, we will explore how feedback control works by looking at a temperature loop on a process vessel, and it is hoped that by the end of it you will have a good overall understanding of the main ideas involved. Essentially, the starting point is the sensor, which is typically a temperature-sensing element placed in the vessel that basically measures the temperature on an ongoing basis and converts what it finds into a signal. This signal is then passed along to the controller, which compares the measured temperature against the desired set point and works out, in a fairly sophisticated way, how far apart the two values are and what sort of corrective action might be appropriate. The controller then sends its output onward to the final element, which is often a control valve on the heating medium line, and this valve actually does the physical work of changing the flow of heating medium so that more or less heat is delivered to the vessel. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, there is the question of the sign of the feedback, which is something that is absolutely fundamental to whether the whole arrangement works at all: the action taken has to oppose the change that triggered it, so that if the temperature rises too high the heating is reduced, and if it falls too low the heating is increased, thereby keeping everything nicely stable overall.
target: A temperature loop on a process vessel holds the vessel temperature at its set point by measuring the temperature and acting on the difference. Four parts make up the loop, and their order matters: sensor, controller, final element, and the sign of the feedback. The sensor is a temperature element in the vessel. The sensor measures the temperature continuously and sends the measurement to the controller as a signal. Measurement is the loop's only contact with the process: every later decision rests on the value the sensor reports, and a sensor that reads high or low displaces the whole loop by that error. The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point and calculates a correction from the difference. The controller does not move anything itself; its output is an instruction, sized by the size of the difference. The final element carries out the instruction. In this loop the final element is a valve on the heating medium line: the valve changes the flow of heating medium, and the changed flow changes the heat delivered to the vessel. Feedback closes the loop because the sensor measures the result of the valve's action and the controller acts again on the new difference. The sign of the feedback decides whether the loop settles or runs away. The action must oppose the change that produced it: a temperature above the set point calls for less heating, a temperature below the set point for more. With the opposite sign, a rise in temperature would call for more heating, the next measurement would be higher still, and the loop would drive the vessel away from the set point it exists to hold.
